title: W07: Exact-candidate commit wrapper, acceptance runner, closure lifecycle
description:
## Context
Up to six agents edit ONE shared checkout on `main` (D-16, no branches/worktrees). Running tests in that shared checkout proves nothing about the tree that actually gets committed (R-21). `./dev commit` therefore serialises the COMMIT BOUNDARY (not the coding): it stages only the agent's files, materialises the exact candidate tree, gates it in isolation, and commits exactly that tree (P11: exact-tree evidence; D-32). W07 also owns `./dev accept` and the bead-closure lifecycle.

## Requirements covered
P11, §11.10 (commit protocol), §11.3 (work loop steps 6–7).

## Area
`xtask`.

## Depends on
W01.

## Design & key rules (the protocol, condensed from §11.10)
1. Acquire an exclusive local commit lock (a real lock). Confirm HEAD on main, no other git op in progress, the bead valid and in_progress (or just-closed for a --close commit), every staged path inside the agent's live reservation. Refuse any unexpected staged path.
2. Stage only the agent's named paths (never `git add -A`). Record parent commit + candidate tree ID.
3. Materialise the tree into the FIXED `.local/candidate/` directory, refreshed in place under the lock; verify the directory's content manifest against the tree — leftover or missing files REFUSE the run (cargo auto-discovers stray tests/*.rs, which would silently test a different tree — D-55). One stable path keeps cargo caches warm; the receipt records the tree ID, never the path. Not a branch, not a linked worktree.
4. Run T0 on the candidate with git discovery DISABLED (GIT_DIR → nonexistent, GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES → candidate root): nothing in there — UBS, cargo VCS info, stray git calls — can see the shared checkout. Changed-file list passed to UBS explicitly; build_id computed from the recorded tree ID (D-74). A fixture proves a git call inside the candidate sees no repository.
5. Re-check parent, tree ID, lock, index; if anything changed, re-run against the new candidate — never commit a different tree because tests already finished.
6. Commit exactly the tested tree; record receipt (tree, parent, bead IDs); release the lock.
- `./dev accept <bead> --tree <id>`: materialises the NAMED committed tree into `.local/accept/<tree-id>/` (content-verified AND git-isolated like the candidate), runs the bead's acceptance selectors there, writes a receipt naming that tree — never a shared checkout, never the commit-locked candidate dir.
- `./dev commit --close <id>`: one-step closure — validates the acceptance receipt, `br close`, `br sync --flush-only`, recomputes requirement activation in registry/requirements.toml, commits .beads/ + that registry file in the same wrapped commit (the wrapper accepts the just-closed bead for this closure commit).
- `./dev commit --close <id> --failed`: records the failure-evidence report, labels the bead failed+needs-owner, leaves it OPEN so dependants stay blocked (critical for the W02 spike; closing a blocker would unblock dependants — D-70).

## Acceptance
- Adversarial fixtures pass: foreign staged path refused; HEAD moving during the gate forces a re-run; a file edited in the shared checkout during the gate is not committed; receipt tree ID equals the committed tree; candidate manifest check refuses leftovers; no branch or worktree ever created. `./dev accept` runs in .local/accept/<tree-id>/ with a receipt naming the tree. `--close` validates receipts, closes the bead and commits .beads/ + registry flips (tested against a FIXTURE registry — W05 provides the real one); `--failed` leaves the bead open with failed/needs-owner. Fixtures cover a missing receipt, a wrong tree ID and a failed spike.

## Out of scope
The real registry gate (W05); gate tier contents (W46); any push behaviour beyond the wrapper hook (a remote does not exist yet — owner action).

## Notes for the future
- A failed gate preserves the agent's work and NEVER cleans up anyone else's edits.
- Commits are serialised (~2-min T0 ⇒ ~30 commits/hour max) — an accepted cost of shared-main development with exact evidence (RISK-19). Keep T0 fast.
- Until this lands, the coordinator-commit bootstrap flow applies (§11.2 step 2); the full swarm launches only after W04+W06+W07.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §11.10, §11.3, D-32, D-55, D-58, D-74, R-21, RISK-5.

title: W08: Config type, genesis fingerprint, limits registry
description:
## Context
One static config file drives everything: cluster identity, membership, addresses, data dirs, semantic limits, timing. It is parsed ONCE into a validated Config type (CD-3) that rejects inconsistent values with specific errors — a config the parser accepts can never fail later at RawNode construction. W08 also builds the semantic-config fingerprint (part of genesis binding, DUR-8) and the limits registry (CD-9: a named, configured maximum on EVERYTHING).

## Requirements covered
O-5 (one static config; no silent default overrides), O-9 (loopback defaults + warning), DUR-8 (genesis binding), CD-3, CD-9.

## Area
`types`, `config` (config/local.toml).

## Depends on
W04 (domain types).

## Design & key rules (validation rules, condensed from §7.10)
Reject, with a specific error: voter count other than 1/3/5 (one odd count per config; release+local profiles pin 5; 1- and 3-voter configs exist for dev/tests/probes/demos — D-45); duplicate/zero node IDs or duplicate client/peer addresses or data dirs; missing cluster ID or protocol version; cross-limit inconsistency — max_key_bytes + max_value_bytes + command envelope must fit the 66 KiB canonical-command limit, which fits the 1 MiB journal-frame and 512 KiB HTTP-body limits; max_journal_bytes ≥ 1.25 × max_history_bytes + max_log_entries × per-entry overhead bound (≈64 B, derived from the frame spec and PINNED BY A TEST) + journal_protocol_allowance (named constant, default 64 MiB) — same formula applies to small test limits so capacity profiles are not flaky; replication in-flight batches × max batch size ≤ per-peer send-queue bytes; node IDs nonzero and below 2^53 (at most 2^53 − 1 = 9007199254740991; D-77, br-s4dg); heartbeat ≥ 1 tick; election-min ≥ 5 × heartbeat; election-max > min; election_max_ticks_exclusive = 2 × election_min_ticks EXACTLY (raft-rs 0.7 hardwires the [t, 2t) range shape — D-75); write deadline ≥ election max; CLI deadline ≥ write_deadline_ticks × tick_ms (reject a shorter CLI deadline, comparing durations in the same units); raft-rs Config::validate constraints honoured so every accepted fixture config constructs a RawNode (proven by a test); every limit within its declared range.
- Timing defaults: tick 50 ms; heartbeat 2 ticks; election [20,40) ticks; write deadline 100 ticks; CLI deadline 15 s. Timers control progress and give-up only — NEVER commitment, versions or history retention.
- Fingerprint (DUR-8/§7.10): covers every parameter that can change a result — key/value limits, live-state limits, history capacity (max_log_entries, max_history_bytes), command-format version, canonical (sorted) voter set. max_journal_bytes is LOCAL, not fingerprinted. Stable across re-parse; changes with every semantic parameter.
- Limits registry (§7.11): every allocation-bearing collection has an entry BEFORE it is introduced; bounded wrapper types; each numeric parameter's allowed range declared alongside its entry and enforced by this parser (OpenAPI and codec limits are checked against the same table — no bound lives in two places).
- Non-loopback address ⇒ prominent unauthenticated-API warning (O-9, RISK-17).

## Acceptance
- Every rejection rule has a test, incl. 1/3/5-voter acceptance and even-count rejection; config/local.toml with 5 nodes parses; fingerprint stable and sensitive to every semantic parameter; bounded wrappers pass N−1/N/N+1 tests; non-loopback warning produced.

## Out of scope
Genesis frame encoding (W11); journal-byte enforcement at runtime (W11/W14).

## Notes for the future
- `data_dir` paths resolve relative to the config file's directory (§7.7 step 0).
- No built-in default may silently override a configured semantic parameter (O-5).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.10, §7.11, DUR-8, D-45, D-68, D-75.

title: W09: State machine — PUT/GET, versions, request history, live-state quota, invariants
description:
## Context
The state machine is the pure heart of keyval: an ordered map plus the never-expiring request history, changed ONLY by the deterministic apply function. Everything else (journal, Raft, HTTP) exists to feed it committed entries in order. This item covers the PUT/GET slice; DELETE/CAS land in W27, SCAN in W28.

## Requirements covered
DM-3 (version = log index of first successful execution; strictly increasing per key incl. across delete/re-create; same-value PUT gets a new version; replay returns the ORIGINAL version; gaps expected), DM-5 (request history: request_id → (first_index, command_digest, terminal_result); NEVER expired or evicted for the life of the cluster), DM-6 (live-state capacity: 10,000 keys / 64 MiB default; over-quota write ⇒ committed terminal `capacity_exceeded`; DELETE and shrinking overwrites always possible), F-1 (PUT), F-2 (GET), F-6 (request-ID semantics), C-6 (each ID takes effect at most once, forever), CD-7 (invariant assertions).

## Area
`statemachine` (crates/statemachine — leaf areas apply later: apply, history, scan, codec).

## Depends on
W04 (types), W08 (limits/config).

## Design & key rules (condensed from §7.5)
- Contents: ordered map key → (value, version); request history; live-state counters (keys, bytes) for DM-6; the committed-command-bytes counter for DM-7 (each FIRST execution adds the canonical encoded command length, whatever its terminal result — mismatch/capacity consume bytes too; replays, conflicts and no-ops add nothing; replay reproduces the counter exactly); applied_index.
- Commands (canonical, versioned byte encoding, ≤ 66 KiB): Put{request_id,key,value}, Delete{request_id,key}, Cas{request_id,key,expected,value}; empty (no-op) entries carry no command.
- Apply(state, index, entry) is PURE and deterministic — the only place writes change state: (1) empty entry → advance applied_index only; (2) decode; a committed entry that fails to decode is an invariant violation (leader validated before proposing); (3) seen request_id: same digest → stored result, nothing changes (replay); different digest → nothing changes, waiters get request_id_conflict, original result stays authoritative; (4) first execution: PUT over DM-6 quota → capacity_exceeded, else set key with version = index; record (index, digest, result) in history INCLUDING mismatch/capacity results (they are terminal); (5) applied_index = index.
- Digest: SHA-256 over canonical command bytes, implemented IN-CRATE (like CRC-32C; no new dependency, CD-12), tested against FIPS 180-4 vectors. Conflict detection rests on collision resistance — a stated Assumption (§10.15), because full command comparison would need disk reads inside apply (R-17).
- Memory: ~120 B per history record ⇒ ~120 MB at the 1M-entry cap — the price of never-expiring retry safety (RISK-4); v2 compaction MUST carry the history.
- No persistence of state-machine state (D-10): rebuilt by replaying the committed log; replay recomputes every result identically because apply is deterministic.
- Invariants (CD-7, via `invariant!` with node/index/invariant-ID context, active in ALL builds): applied_index ≤ commit_index; a key's version never decreases; bounded collections never exceed their limit.

## Acceptance
- Property tests: version = execution index; a replay returns the original result; a conflicting digest changes nothing; the quota outcome is terminal and deterministic; corrupted-state fixtures FIRE the assertions (prove the invariants are armed, not decorative).

## Out of scope
DELETE/CAS (W27), SCAN (W28), status endpoint semantics (W29), journal encoding (W11 owns frames; the command codec lives here as statemachine/codec).

## Notes for the future
- A different agent should write the reference model (W10) from §6/§8 prose — never from this code (independent authorship, §11.7; RISK-8).
- The DM-7 byte counter is read at the leader's applied index for admission (W14/W29) — keep it exact under replay (a test proves identical accounting after recovery).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.5, D-07, D-10, D-13, R-15, R-17, RISK-4.

title: W10: Reference model, observation schema, differential tests
description:
## Context
Checkers must never compute expected results with the code under test (D-21, RISK-8). The reference model is a deliberately simple, obviously correct, single-threaded in-memory model of keyval's semantics — the oracle for checkers K-4/K-5/K-10, the differential property tests, and (W30) the model server the conformance suite validates against. Written FROM §6 and §8 prose, ideally by a different agent than W09's author.

## Requirements covered
T-7 (reference model defines expected semantics), T-12 (oracle independence: depends on NO production crate, not even domain types — defines its own small key/value types; consumes the documented observation schema), §10.14.

## Area
`model` (crates/model).

## Depends on
W03 (spec), W09 (the differential test needs the state machine to diff against — the model itself is written from prose).

## Design & key rules
- The model: ordered map + request history; applies commands one at a time in log order; returns exactly what the API promises — version, existed, CAS success/mismatch with current version, replay, conflict, capacity outcomes, SCAN pages. No consensus, no I/O, no cleverness.
- The observation schema (versioned, in schemas/): the documented format in which the harness records invocations, responses, first executions etc.; the model reads commands from it. This schema is the contract between the sim/workload side (W36) and the whole oracle stack (W38–W40) — design it here, carefully.
- Differential property tests (T0): random command sequences applied to BOTH the state machine and the model; results and final states must match. For this item PUT/GET pass; DELETE/CAS/SCAN rows are registered as `planned` (reported, not enforced) until W27/W28.
- Disagreement between model and state machine: the PLAN (§6/§8) decides which is wrong; a model bug is fixed like a checker bug — `conflict` + `needs-owner` bead with an independent counterexample (§11.5 rule 3).

## Acceptance
- The model covers every operation and outcome in §6/§8; the dependency check proves no production dependencies; the differential test passes for PUT/GET (others planned); a deliberately broken state-machine variant FAILS the differential test (proves the oracle has teeth).

## Out of scope
The model HTTP server (W30); checkers themselves (W38–W40).

## Notes for the future
- B-22 (W45) will mutate this model in a sandboxed copy and expect fixture suites to catch it.
- Keep it boring: every clever optimisation here is a place a shared conceptual bug can hide (RISK-8).

title: W11: Journal engine — frames, genesis, logical truncation, offset index, entry cache, recovery
description:
## Context
The journal is the ONE durable authority (CD-10, D-10): an append-only framed file per node; everything else (key-value map, request history) is derived by replay. Raft is only safe if entries and votes are synced before the node acts on them — this engine provides the frames, recovery and fail-closed guarantees that make that true.

## Requirements covered
DUR-1 (ack only after commit+apply — journal side), DUR-4 (no compaction in v1), DUR-5 (format version + golden vectors), DUR-6 (torn tail discarded; corruption refuses; never silently repair synced data), DUR-8 (genesis binding), DUR-9 (recovery correct under the stated crash model), CD-9, CD-10.

## Area
`journal` (crates/journal, incl. golden/ vectors).

## Depends on
W04 (types/ports), W08 (config, fingerprint).

## Design & key rules (condensed from §7.6–§7.7)
- One append-only `journal.log` + `LOCK` file (exclusive data-directory ownership).
- Frame layout (little-endian): magic `KVJ1` (4B) | format version (2B) | kind (1B: Genesis|RaftBatch) | reserved zero (1B) | payload length (4B, ≤ 1 MiB) | frame sequence (8B, strictly increasing) | HEADER checksum (CRC-32C over the fixed header fields — lets the resync scan trust an intact header's length, D-69) | payload | checksum (CRC-32C over header+payload) | trailing length (4B, = payload length; detects incomplete final frames).
- Records: Genesis{format_version, instance_id (random 128-bit, stamped at init), cluster_id (display only), node_id, voters, semantic_config_fingerprint} — always frame 1; RaftBatch{entries[], hard_state?} — one per persisted Ready.
- Logical truncation: a RaftBatch whose first entry index ≤ current last index REPLACES the logical log from that index; old bytes stay (append-only); replacing at or below the persisted commit index is an invariant violation.
- Offset index in memory: LogIndex → (offset, term), ~16 B/entry, bounded by DM-7. Entry cache: bounded (8 MiB); misses read via the byte-storage port in bounded chunks; eviction changes cost, never results.
- CRC-32C implemented in-crate, tested against standard vectors (CD-12). Detects accidents, not adversaries.
- FAIL CLOSED recovery scan: first invalid frame ends the durable prefix at last valid frame N; then a RESYNC SCAN over the ENTIRE remainder (bounded-memory chunks) searches at every byte offset for a complete checksum-valid frame with sequence > N: found ⇒ damage inside the durable prefix ⇒ CORRUPTION, refuse (covers corrupted mid-journal frame with valid N+2 after it, and sequence gaps); none ⇒ torn tail, discarded AND physically truncated (through the port's Truncate, then synced) before the next append. Lengths in a damaged tail are untrusted UNLESS the header checksum validates (an intact torn frame's header gives a trustworthy length; the scan skips its payload range, so client bytes in a torn payload cannot masquerade as a later frame — residual crafted-payload case is a stated Assumption, D-69). A legitimate torn tail is ≤ one maximum frame (because §7.4 keeps at most one Ready unsynced); longer trailing region ⇒ corruption, refuse.
- Recovery sequence (§7.7): lock → genesis verify (node ID, voters, fingerprint; load instance ID) → scan → rebuild logical log/offset index/hard state → replay 1..commit through ordinary apply → construct Raft with applied position → Ready. Ordinary start REFUSES a missing directory or missing genesis (blank rejoin = Raft amnesia, D-52). `init` may re-run only while the journal holds no complete genesis and nothing after it.
- Golden vectors (committed byte files, each with a README line): encoded genesis + RaftBatch (decode→expected; encode→identical bytes); recovery cases: empty journal; clean; incomplete final frame cut mid-header/mid-payload/mid-trailer (discard); bad checksum on final complete frame (discard as torn); zero-filled tail; garbage/bad-magic tail (discard); bad checksum mid-journal with valid continuation (refuse via resync); corrupted N+1 followed by valid N+2 (refuse); sequence gap with valid continuation (refuse); trailing region longer than one max frame (refuse); logical truncation + replacements; truncation below commit (refuse); crash during physical tail truncation (recovery converges); incomplete genesis-only journal (recoverable only by explicit init).
- Goldens are ORACLES (P9): a format change bumps the format version, adds NEW goldens, records in §16. NEVER regenerate goldens to make a test pass.

## Acceptance
- Every §7.6 golden vector passes; recovery returns hard state and logical log; fail-closed cases refuse with specific errors; cache eviction never changes results.

## Out of scope
The real-file and simulated byte-storage adapters (W12); the Ready loop that produces frames (W13); crash probes (W24).

## Notes for the future
- DUR-2 nuance: entries, TERM and VOTE are synced before dependent messages; the COMMIT INDEX is volatile — persisted only opportunistically inside a frame being written anyway, never worth a frame alone (D-44; frame-stream identity everywhere depends on this rule).
- The crash model (single definition §10.2): a PREFIX of the unsynced append survives (none/some/all), optionally followed by zero/garbage bytes up to the append's extent, never longer than one max frame; synced bytes never damaged. Recovery fails closed on anything outside it (§10.15 Assumption).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.6, §7.7, §10.2, D-50, D-52, D-60, D-63, D-69.

title: W12: Byte-storage adapters — real files and simulated disk, one contract suite
description:
## Context
The byte-storage port has two adapters — real files (production) and the simulated disk (volatile + durable byte images) — and ONE shared contract test suite that both must pass (P3: what simulation proves must hold for production). The simulated disk is where the crash model lives: a seed-chosen prefix of unsynced bytes survives, optionally followed by garbage.

## Requirements covered
DUR-1, DUR-7 (directory durability: created files volatile until parent dir synced), DUR-9 (crash model), T-2 (same engine code against both adapters).

## Area
`fs_storage` (real-file adapter), `sim/disk` (leaf area of crates/sim).

## Depends on
W11 (journal engine defines usage), W15 (the sim crate and its facade are created by W15 — D-74 orders W15 before W12).

## Design & key rules
- Contract suite: append, read_at (bounded), Truncate (relied on only after its own sync), Sync(seq) → SyncDone(seq, incarnation), create-file + sync-directory, exclusive lock. Runs identically against both adapters.
- Simulated disk (§10.2): per-node volatile and durable byte images; appends land volatile; sync makes durable. On crash a seed-chosen portion of unsynced appended bytes survives as a prefix — none, some or all — optionally followed by zero or garbage bytes up to the append's extent (the seed chooses; never ONLY "all unsynced bytes vanish"). Directory entries modelled: a created file stays volatile until the parent directory is synced (crash between create and dir-sync loses the file). Truncate uses the same volatile/durable split incl. crash between truncation and its sync. A sync can become durable while its completion notification is lost to a crash; the scheduler sometimes delivers the stale completion to the NEXT incarnation, which must ignore it (B-17's fuel). Synced bytes are never damaged (corruption deferred, §9.2). Reads are instantaneous and deterministic.
- Real-file adapter: real fsync/fdatasync; syncs the parent directory on create (DUR-7); exclusive lock refuses a second process. Used by the server, CLI doctor and the crash probes.

## Acceptance
- One contract suite runs against both adapters; the simulated disk covers partial unsynced survival (none/some/all), a lost sync completion, directory-entry volatility until directory sync, and a crash during Truncate; the file adapter syncs directories on create and its lock refuses a second process.

## Out of scope
Failpoint instrumentation and SIGKILL probes (W24 adds them inside fs_storage behind the `failpoints` feature); the simulator scheduler (W15).

## Notes for the future
- Keep fs_storage thin — adapters only translate (CD-1). The sync-order check (W24) will instrument BELOW this adapter at the OS-call boundary.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.2 (byte storage), §10.2 (simulated disk), DUR-7/9, D-50, D-74.

title: W13: raft-rs adapter and the Ready loop — the critical persistence protocol
description:
## Context
The second stop/go point. This is the single most dangerous piece of code in the project (RISK-2): the adapter that drives the vendored raft-rs RawNode through the Ready loop, deciding exactly WHEN bytes are synced and WHEN messages are released. The most common way replicated systems lose acknowledged data is releasing a vote, acknowledgement or client reply before the state it depends on is durable. v1 takes the maximally conservative path (D-28): one serial controller, ONE outstanding Ready, sync before releasing ANY message, no pipelining.

## Requirements covered
C-1 (linearizable writes), C-2 (acknowledged writes never lost), DUR-2 (entries, term and vote synced BEFORE any dependent message — vote grants and append acks included; commit index is VOLATILE, persisted only opportunistically).

## Area
`raft_adapter` (crates/raft_adapter).

## Depends on
W02 (the spike must be GO; vendored+patched library), W11 (journal engine for persistence).

## Design & key rules — THE READY LOOP (normative, §7.4)
1. Feed ONE input (tick | peer message | proposal). Reads/status never touch the library.
2. Take one Ready. A Ready containing a snapshot is an invariant violation (v1 never compacts).
3. Persist: encode new entries + hard-state change into ONE journal frame, append, sync. A Ready with nothing to persist (no entries, no hard-state change beyond commit index — library's must_sync false) writes NO frame (commit index alone is never worth a frame — fixed so frame streams, goldens, K-11 obligations and byte accounting are identical everywhere). Until SyncDone: no further library input; reads keep serving from the current published view; ticks accumulate in a pending counter; deadline bookkeeping still advances. SyncDone is an I/O completion — NEVER dropped by admission bounds.
4. After SyncDone: expose new entries to the library's storage view (offset index + cache), THEN release ALL the Ready's messages in recorded order (v1 holds even messages the library would allow earlier).
5. Apply committed entries in index order; published view advances one complete entry at a time; waiting client attempts complete on apply.
6. Advance; handle LightReady (send its messages — obligations already met; apply its committed entries). If has_ready immediately (committed entries held by the per-Ready bound, fresh leader messages), loop to step 2 and DRAIN before the next input: committed work never waits on an idle input queue.
7. Report applied progress only for entries actually applied.
Rules: never release a vote grant or append ack on unsynced state; never turn queued/proposed/stored/sent into client success; the library's commit rule is authoritative (NO home-grown majority counting); a commit-index advance from LightReady need not be persisted before applying; SyncDone from a previous incarnation is ignored; at most one input between Readys ⇒ one Ready persists ≤ one append batch (≤256 KiB) or one proposal (≤66 KiB) + hard state ⇒ every frame ≤ 1 MiB and a torn tail ≤ one frame (the frame encoder asserts this).
- Consensus port: propose/step/tick/ready/advance/query (role, term, leader, indices). NO library type crosses the port (CD-1) — replacing the library may not change state machine, API, CLI or checkers.
- Configuration: pre-vote ON, check-quorum ON, explicit logger (no background thread), batch/in-flight limits from §7.11 incl. max_committed_size_per_ready = 1 MiB (raft-rs leaves it unlimited by default!).
- initial_state (raft-rs Storage contract): recovered hard state + ConfState from the configured static voter set — membership never comes from the log in v1 (§7.7 step 6).
- Peer-envelope codec + identity validation live HERE (D-71): envelopes carry instance ID, protocol version, semantic fingerprint, sender and destination node IDs; all five validated before stepping Raft; mismatches dropped and counted. The simulated network (W16) and HTTP transport (W21) use this identical code (P3).
- Exact 0.7.0 API calls (advance / advance_append / advance_apply; ordinary vs persisted message lists) verified against the pinned API with adversarial ordering tests.

## Acceptance
- Adversarial ordering tests: no message leaves before its sync; LightReady messages/entries handled; one outstanding Ready; snapshot Ready = invariant failure; old-incarnation SyncDone ignored; initial_state maps recovered hard state + static ConfState; a large-log election/commit test bounds memory (per the W02 audit findings); envelope codec round-trip + mismatch-drop tests; 1- and 3-voter in-memory clusters commit and apply.

## Out of scope
The node controller/request lifecycle (W14); HTTP transport wiring (W21); bug variants B-16/B-17 (W45 injects them HERE, never in vendor).

## Notes for the future
- K-11 (W40) will deterministically audit every vote grant/append-ack/success against its sync obligations from the trace — the loop's obligations ARE DUR-2's: entries, term, vote; never the commit index (D-44).
- If raft-rs must be replaced (fallback OpenRaft), only this crate and a journal/peer-codec migration change — that isolation is the point of the port.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.3, §7.4, §8.2 (envelope), D-28, D-44, D-71, RISK-2.

title: W14: Node controller — request lifecycle, fixed decision order, reads, effects
description:
## Context
The node controller is the serial brain of each node: it owns the request lifecycle (the attempt state machine), the fixed write decision order, local reads, effect emission and deadline bookkeeping. One controller turn at a time; everything observable happens through effects (CD-1). This item covers the PUT/GET rows; the CAS-mismatch/conflict/capacity rows are accepted in W27/W29.

## Requirements covered
F-7 (routing/decision order), A-2 (reads on any ready node), A-5 (unknown-outcome honesty), C-3 (reads reflect an applied committed prefix), C-4 (per-incarnation read monotonicity).

## Area
`node` (crates/node; leaf areas node/lifecycle, node/write_path, node/reads, node/effects).

## Depends on
W09 (state machine), W13 (Consensus port).

## Design & key rules
- FIXED write decision order (F-7), identical on every node: parse/validate (F-8, no side effects) → lifecycle (non-Ready ⇒ `recovering`) → local admission bounds (`busy`) → SHORT-CIRCUIT from the local applied history (any Ready node answers a known request ID locally — same digest ⇒ original result replayed:true; different ⇒ request_id_conflict; NEVER redirects a known retry) → ATTACH to a pending same-ID same-digest proposal (bounded waiters; a same-ID different-digest attempt never attaches — waits, then is evaluated against committed history) → leader check (no leader ⇒ `unavailable` + node list; non-leader ⇒ 307 + Location) → history admission (`history_full`, DM-7, read from commit index + applied byte counter) → uncommitted-bytes bound (`busy`) → propose.
- Attempt lifecycle (CD-2): NotSubmitted → (Submitted, marked BEFORE handing to the library) → Terminal(on apply of an entry carrying this ID with this digest). Deadline/leadership-loss/shutdown ⇒ 504 unknown_outcome (attempt_state submitted); a synchronous ProposalDropped with nothing appended reclassifies NotSubmitted ⇒ 429 busy (A-5: only never-submitted attempts may say not_submitted).
- Reads (§7.9): GET and status lookups answered in ONE serial turn from the published view; response copied (bounded) before any later apply can change it; served_by{node_id, applied_index} attached; non-Ready ⇒ 503 recovering, never an invented or partial state. Reads and short-circuits are answered even while a Ready's sync is outstanding; attach/propose queue behind it.
- Ticks: write deadline counted in TICKS from admission (identical in simulation); overdue ticks processed in batches ≤ 8/turn interleaved with other inputs (pause handling); deadline bookkeeping advances on every input even while Raft inputs are deferred, so deadlines always fire.
- Effects in deterministic order; incarnation discipline on completions.

## Acceptance
- The PUT/GET lifecycle rows of the §7.8 attempt table and their §8.4 paths (not_leader, busy, unavailable, recovering, unknown_outcome, replay, attach, short-circuit, F-7 order) driven by tests through core inputs; attach requires a matching digest; deadline and leadership loss give unknown_outcome; recovering until ready; reads succeed on any ready node and carry served_by.

## Out of scope
CAS/DELETE semantics (W27), SCAN (W28), status endpoint + full retry/ambiguity acceptance (W29), HTTP parsing (W18).

## Notes for the future
- "Never turn queued/proposed/stored/sent into client success" — only APPLY completes an attempt (DUR-1).
- C-4 is per node INCARNATION, judged in response-GENERATION order (the trace records it); after restart a node may briefly report an older prefix — that is legal.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.8, §7.9, §7.12 (serial controller), F-7, A-5, D-35.

title: W15: Simulation scheduler, entropy streams, canonical trace, K-14 replay identity
description:
## Context
The FoundationDB-style simulator starts here: a single-threaded discrete-event scheduler, seeded entropy streams, and the canonical trace that makes determinism CHECKABLE. W15 creates the `sim` crate and its facade (D-74 — which is why W12's sim-disk work depends on W15).

## Requirements covered
T-3 (byte-identical traces), T-5 (god view), T-11 (fresh-process replay), P4; owns checker K-14 (replay identity — a stated T-12 exemption: it lives in the sim crate, compares traces byte-for-byte, consults no expected-result oracle).

## Area
`sim` (crates/sim; leaf areas sim/scheduler, sim/trace — net/disk/nemesis/workload/shrinker come later).

## Depends on
W04 (ports/types).

## Design & key rules
- Scheduler: priority queue ordered by (virtual_time, seeded_tie_priority, insertion_sequence) — the seeded tie priority varies simultaneous-event order between seeds; the insertion sequence makes order total.
- Entropy: independent streams split from the master seed — clients, network, disk, faults, scheduler, and each node's entropy port (per node AND per incarnation). Observing a run never consumes protocol randomness (otherwise adding a log line would change elections).
- Canonical trace: event order, packet bytes/endpoints, disk ops/completions, role+term observations, log/commit/apply changes, client invocations/responses, first executions, checker verdicts, deterministic metrics. Fixed field ordering and integer formats. EXCLUDES host PIDs, wall-clock, paths, memory addresses, irrelevant diagnostics — and never excludes an inconvenient protocol decision. Hash accelerates comparison; on mismatch both full traces are kept and the FIRST DIFFERING EVENT is reported.
- K-14 replay identity: fresh OS processes, same binary + manifest, compare event counts and complete canonical traces (not just final states). Registered with marker + selector.
- Event budget: 1,000,000 events per run (manifest); exhaustion reports `incomplete` which FAILS (P10).
- Run manifest: scenario_version, seed, profile, build_id (source tree + toolchain + target + lockfile + features + raft patch), config fingerprint, prng name/version, max_events, chaos/heal budgets.

## Acceptance
- Event ordering with seeded tie priority; per-subsystem entropy streams; trace encoding excludes host data; fresh-process replay comparison with a first-divergence report, registered as checker K-14 with marker and selector; the sim crate + facade created; event-budget exhaustion reports incomplete.

## Out of scope
Network (W16), composition root (W17), nemesis/workload (W36/W37), campaigns/crash packs (W42).

## Notes for the future
- The trace is the foundation for K-11 (persistence-ordering audits) and all replay tooling; design the event vocabulary with those consumers in mind (W10.2's observation schema is the client-facing cousin).
- Any nondeterminism found later is a P0 (RISK-6); B-19 (ambient randomness in one node) must be CAUGHT by K-14 with a reliable changing-counter fixture, not a "might differ" test.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.2, §10.7, K-14 (§10.5), D-14, D-34, D-74.

title: W16: Simulated network — partitions, loss, delay, reorder, duplication
description:
## Context
The simulated network: the fault surface for partitions, loss, delay, reorder and duplication, carrying the SAME encoded peer envelopes as production through bounded queues (P3 — the envelope codec comes from W13, D-71).

## Requirements covered
§9.1 (the in-scope fault model, network side).

## Area
`sim/net` (leaf area of crates/sim).

## Depends on
W13 (peer-envelope codec), W15 (scheduler).

## Design & key rules
- Per-message delay distribution; drop and duplicate probabilities; delivery follows delay, not send order (reordering is the default, FIFO is never assumed — §9.3).
- A directed link matrix for symmetric AND asymmetric partitions (3/2, 4/1, 2/2/1, leader-can-send-but-not-receive, directed cycles).
- Client-response paths can also lose/delay messages (losing the reply after a committed application is a required scenario — it feeds unknown-outcome and retry testing).
- Packets are NOT tied to incarnations: stale packets may arrive after a restart and must be handled as ordinary stale protocol messages (only process-local completions are incarnation-filtered).
- Bounded per-peer queues (64 msgs / 8 MiB): overflow drops and counts as a network failure, never grows.

## Acceptance
- Directed partitions, loss, delay, reorder, duplication and bounded queues each have a scenario test; carries the real peer-envelope codec from W13; stale packets are delivered across a restart; client-response loss supported.

## Out of scope
Fault SCHEDULING policy (the nemesis, W37) — this item provides the mechanisms.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.2 (simulated network), §9.1, D-71.

title: W18: Production root — keyval-server (init + run), single node, PUT/GET over HTTP
description:
## Context
The production composition root: `keyval-server`, one OS process per node, async runtime CONFINED to this crate and its adapters. First as a single real 1-voter node (D-45 allows 1/3/5-voter configs; release/local pin 5) serving durable PUT/GET over real HTTP with real files.

## Requirements covered
F-1, F-2 (PUT/GET), O-1 (health live/ready + /v1/cluster), O-3 (structured JSON-lines logs, bounded queue, counted drops), O-9 (loopback defaults), DUR-3 (recovery without operator action), §7.7 step 0 (explicit init).

## Area
`server` (crates/server).

## Depends on
W03 (spec), W08 (config), W12 (fs adapter), W14 (controller).

## Design & key rules
- `keyval-server init --config <file> --node <id> --instance <hex>`: initialises a data directory per §7.7 step 0, built on the journal genesis writer — create dir, sync parent, take lock, create journal.log + sync dir, write+sync genesis (instance ID, display cluster ID, node ID, voters, fingerprint). `run` REFUSES an uninitialised or missing directory (anti-amnesia, D-52).
- One serial controller task owns the core; client attempts, peer messages, ticks and I/O completions arrive through ONE bounded input queue; completions bypass the admission bound so a waiting Ready always resolves; file writes/syncs run off the controller and return as SyncDone; deadline bookkeeping advances on every input (§7.12).
- HTTP adapter: parses into domain types at the boundary (CD-3; strict JSON, query-key decoding incl. the reject-unescaped-plus rule), submits ClientRequest; each Respond effect completes the HTTP response; a lost connection after submission is just an unresolved attempt — nothing rolls back.
- Health: live (lifecycle starting/recovering/ready/failed), ready (200 only with a complete committed read view); /v1/cluster (node id, cluster id, role, term, leader, durable last index, commit index, applied index, peers + match_index where known).
- Thin by design: adapters only translate; no consensus/state-machine/request logic outside the core (CD-1, R-24).

## Acceptance
- init initialises per §7.7 step 0 and run refuses an uninitialised directory; a real 1-voter node serves PUT/GET per the spec; health live/ready + /v1/cluster work; structured logs; data survives a direct kill and restart of the process (PID-receipt start/kill/restart helpers sufficient for ONE node — the full launcher is W22); loopback by default.

## Out of scope
Peer transport and routing (W21), the 5-node launcher (W22), DELETE/CAS/SCAN/status handlers (W32).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.12, §7.7 step 0, D-52, D-65, R-24.

title: W21: Peer transport, five-node config, write routing (307/503)
description:
## Context
From one real node to five real processes: the HTTP peer transport (each node's separate peer address, `POST /raft`), the five-node static config in production, and write routing — the visible F-7 behaviours 307-to-leader and 503-with-node-list.

## Requirements covered
F-7 (routing), A-1 (writes eventually succeed in the healthy envelope — real-cluster side), A-3 (automatic re-election), O-5 (one static config).

## Area
`server`.

## Depends on
W18 (single-node server).

## Design & key rules
- The peer channel is INTERNAL: bounded envelopes of encoded Raft messages on the peer address; excluded from the public API contract and the conformance suite.
- Identity validation uses W13's codec UNCHANGED (D-71, P3): instance ID, protocol version, semantic fingerprint, sender and destination node IDs all validated before Raft sees a message; mismatches dropped with a counted error — two accidentally connected clusters can never exchange Raft traffic. W21 only WIRES the transport.
- Bounded per-peer send queues (64 msgs / 8 MiB): drop and count; config validation already guarantees ordinary catch-up bursts fit (in-flight × batch ≤ queue bytes).
- Routing: a write to a follower that passes earlier F-7 steps gets HTTP 307 with `Location` = the believed leader's URL for the SAME path and query (re-encoding exactly the same decoded bytes) + typed not_leader body; with no leader known: 503 unavailable with all configured client addresses.

## Acceptance
- Five real processes elect and replicate; a write to a follower gets 307 with the leader's Location; with no leader, 503 unavailable lists the nodes; a peer envelope with a mismatched instance ID, protocol version, fingerprint, or sender/destination node ID is dropped and counted.

## Out of scope
The launcher (W22); DELETE/CAS/SCAN handlers (W32).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §8.2 (peer channel), F-7, D-09, D-71.
acceptance_criteria: Five real processes elect and replicate; follower write gets 307 with leader Location; no leader gives 503 with node list; envelope mismatches (all five fields) dropped and counted

title: W22: Cluster launcher and lifecycle commands (./dev cluster ...)
description:
## Context
The operator surface for real clusters: `./dev cluster init|up|status|kill|restart|down`. Safety is the design driver: the launcher signals ONLY processes it started (PID receipts), never kills by port, never uses broad pkill, never deletes data (O-2). Gates will start ephemeral clusters hourly, so every subcommand takes `--config` (default config/local.toml) and per-run configs with fresh directories are first-class (D-63).

## Requirements covered
O-2 (launcher), O-3 (logs — one file per node).

## Area
`xtask`.

## Depends on
W21 (five-node server).

## Design & key rules
- `init`: generates ONE random 128-bit cluster instance ID and stamps all five data directories with it (calling keyval-server init per node); refuses directories that ever held data (re-init is owner-only, outside every gate); fresh per-run directories MAY be auto-initialised by gates/tests.
- `up`: starts five processes from the static config; refuses uninitialised directories; records PID receipts. `status`: per-node liveness/role. `kill --node N` / `restart --node N`: SIGKILL semantics for probes; signals only receipted PIDs; refuses foreign processes or occupied ports. `down`: stops everything it started.
- Destructive re-initialisation is NEVER a gate action; cluster commands never delete data. The owner cluster and arbitrary node directories are always protected. The explicit Q9 exception permits only ./dev prune to retire generated per-run .local/gates/ and .local/accept/ artifacts under §10.10 retention, after their receipted processes are stopped; it never reinitialises a used directory.

## Acceptance
- init/up/status/kill/restart/down work, each accepting --config (per-run gate configs included); init generates and stamps the cluster instance ID; PID receipts; refuses to signal a foreign process or use an occupied port; never deletes data.

## Out of scope
The probes themselves (W24); scheduling (W46).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: O-2, §7.7 step 0, D-63, D-65.

title: W23: keyval CLI crate with offline doctor
description:
## Context
`keyval doctor <data-dir>`: offline verification of a node's data directory — cheap, high-value durability assurance (D-26). Also creates the `keyval` CLI crate that W33 later fills with client commands.

## Requirements covered
O-7 (doctor), O-6 (--json with versioned schema).

## Area
`cli` (crates/cli).

## Depends on
W11 (journal/recovery logic), W12 (fs adapter).

## Design & key rules
- Verifies offline: genesis record, frame checksums, sequence and index contiguity, term monotonicity, hard-state consistency (commit ≤ last index).
- Probes the data-directory LOCK FIRST and refuses a live (locked) directory — otherwise in-flight appends would be misread as damage.
- Reports what startup recovery WOULD do (e.g. "discard 37-byte incomplete final frame") without modifying anything — doctor is strictly read-only, proven by hashing the directory before/after.

## Acceptance
- Correct verdict on every journal golden recovery case; never modifies files (checked by hashing the directory); --json validates against its schema.

## Out of scope
Client commands put/get/delete/cas/scan/status/pending/resume (W33).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: O-7, D-26.

title: W24: Real-file crash probes, sync-order check, five-node lifecycle smoke
description:
## Context
Simulated bytes cannot prove the real file adapter drives real files correctly (D-33). W24 adds the fixed set of real-process checks: SIGKILL crash probes at defined write/sync boundaries, the syscall-level sync-order check, and the five-node lifecycle smoke test. HONEST LIMIT (D-46): SIGKILL does not drop the OS page cache, so unsynced bytes survive the kill and a missing fsync cannot be detected this way — these are process-crash probes, not power-loss tests. The sync-order check closes part of that gap; power-loss durability itself is a recorded Assumption ("the filesystem and disk honour fsync"), with dm-log-writes/LazyFS as a v2 option.

## Requirements covered
DUR-1, DUR-3, DUR-7, DUR-9, T-14.

## Area
`fs_storage` (probe tests), `xtask`.

## Depends on
W12 (fs adapter), W22 (cluster lifecycle for the smoke test), W23 (doctor used afterwards).

## Design & key rules
- Crash probes: a child process runs the real journal + file adapter against a real temp directory. Test-only FAILPOINTS — confined to the fs_storage crate (outside the deterministic core), behind a `failpoints` feature proven OFF in release builds (with bug-variants, the only two sanctioned test-only features; T-2/T-6) — let the parent SIGKILL it at each boundary: before a write; mid-append; after write before sync; after sync before the completion is observed; during directory creation; during tail truncation. The parent restarts it and checks: every synced frame present; torn tail discarded; nothing in the durable prefix damaged; recovery never erases synced data; a second process cannot take the lock while the first holds it.
- Sync-order check: a thin OS-call trait INSIDE fs_storage with a recording test implementation at the syscall boundary asserts the real fsync/fdatasync and directory-sync calls for every §7.4 and DUR-7 obligation actually happened, IN ORDER (a port-level wrapper would only prove the engine requested syncs, not that the adapter issued them).
- Lifecycle smoke: against a real local 5-node cluster — write N acknowledged keys; SIGKILL the leader and one follower via ./dev cluster kill; restart them; wait until ALL FIVE nodes report applied index ≥ the last acknowledged write's index via /v1/cluster (waiting only for the restarted ones leaves lagging followers to fail the read check spuriously); verify every acknowledged key from every node (via a minimal in-crate HTTP client); ./dev cluster down; then keyval doctor on every STOPPED data directory.
- Each probe gets a scripted twin in the simulator; observable outcomes must agree (checked by W48).

## Acceptance
- SIGKILL at every §10.17 boundary recovers correctly; the sync-order check asserts every §7.4/DUR-7 obligation was issued in order; lock contention refused; the five-node smoke passes end to end per §10.17.

## Out of scope
A general random real-process fault framework (v2); power-loss emulation (v2).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.17, D-33, D-46, T-14.
acceptance_criteria:
SIGKILL at every boundary recovers correctly; sync-order check proves every sync obligation issued in order; lock contention refused; five-node smoke passes incl. all-five catch-up wait, per-node key verification and doctor on stopped dirs
- [ ] Probe and smoke scripts log every step per the W01.6 standard; a probe failure prints the boundary hit, a data-directory state summary and the recovery verdict so diagnosis needs no debugger

title: W27: DELETE and COMPARE_SWAP (terminal mismatch, mismatch-before-capacity)
description:
## Context
DELETE and COMPARE_SWAP complete the mutation set. CAS is the reason this is a CP system (D-01): it needs one agreed order of writes. The subtle parts are all about TERMINALITY: a CAS mismatch is a committed, terminal decision that consumes the request ID (D-35) — retrying returns the same mismatch; comparing against newer state needs a NEW request ID.

## Requirements covered
F-3 (DELETE: removes, returns existed; deleting absent succeeds with existed=false), F-5 (CAS with expected absent|version; mismatch returns current version/absence, changes nothing, is terminal; a matching CAS is then subject to the DM-6 check exactly like PUT — mismatch evaluated STRICTLY BEFORE capacity), C-5 (CAS evaluated at application, never admission), DM-3 (versions strictly increase incl. across delete/re-create; DELETE and failed CAS assign no version).

## Area
`statemachine/apply`, `node/write_path` (leaf-module reservations so W27/W28/W29 can run concurrently).

## Depends on
W09 (state machine core), W10 (model, for differential tests), W14 (controller write path).

## Design & key rules
- Apply step 4 extensions: DELETE → remove if present, result `existed`; CAS → expectation mismatch ⇒ version_mismatch(current) (terminal, recorded in history); match but over DM-6 quota ⇒ capacity_exceeded (also terminal, recorded); else set with version = index. The reference model implements the same order — mismatch-before-capacity is part of the contract.
- CAS expectation type is Absent | Version(v) (CD-2) — "absent" is a first-class expectation, not a null.
- If a key was deleted and re-created, its new version cannot equal any old one (versions are log indices) — a stale CAS can never accidentally succeed (walk-through §9.5).
- Node write path: CAS admission does NO evaluation (C-5); mismatch surfaces only on apply.

## Acceptance
- Absent/present DELETE; absent/match/mismatch CAS with terminal mismatch; mismatch-before-capacity order on a matching CAS over quota; versions strictly increase across delete and re-create; CAS never evaluated at admission; differential tests against the model pass for both operations (the W10 planned rows flip to enforced).

## Out of scope
SCAN (W28), status/attach/conflict acceptance rows (W29), HTTP handlers (W32).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.5 step 4, F-3/F-5, C-5, D-35, §9.5.

title: W28: SCAN — stateless pagination, exact byte caps, one prefix per page
description:
## Context
SCAN: stateless range pagination (D-29) — no server-side cursors, no snapshot lifetimes, bounded responses even with 64 KiB values. Each page is computed from ONE applied prefix (C-8); the accumulation rule is exact and implemented INDEPENDENTLY three times (core, reference model, K-5 checker — T-12) so a shared bug cannot hide.

## Requirements covered
F-4, C-8, DM-4 (byte-wise lexicographic order of UTF-8 encodings).

## Area
`statemachine/scan`, `node/reads`.

## Depends on
W09, W10, W14.

## Design & key rules (condensed from §8.5/§7.11)
- Range [start, end), byte-wise UTF-8 order; omitted bounds unbounded; start > end invalid; equal bounds ⇒ empty page; empty-string key invalid even as a bound (omit instead).
- `after`: exclusive continuation bound, intersected with the range; after ≥ end ⇒ empty page.
- Page caps: at most `limit` items (1–128, default 32) AND at most 1 MiB of DECODED key+value bytes. Exact accumulation rule: sum len(key)+len(value) in decoded bytes over returned items; stop BEFORE the item that would exceed either cap; ALWAYS return the first item (one maximum-size item always fits); next_after and probe-item bytes never count. The caps are fixed semantic constants (part of the fingerprint).
- has_more true iff another in-range key existed beyond the returned items IN THAT PAGE'S VIEW; then next_after = exactly the last returned key, else null.
- Pages may come from different prefixes or nodes; keys inserted/deleted between pages may be missed or appear; a normally continued traversal never returns the same key twice. No multi-page snapshot (R-16).
- One serial controller turn per page; the response is copied before any later application (C-8: a page never mixes two prefixes).

## Acceptance
- Range edges, after continuation, item and decoded-byte caps, one prefix per page; an INDEPENDENT byte-order Unicode fixture (composed vs decomposed, multibyte ordering); differential tests against the model pass.

## Out of scope
HTTP handler (W32); K-5's independent re-implementation (W39).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §8.5, §7.11 (SCAN row), C-8, D-29, D-75, R-16.

title: W29: Request status and the full retry/ambiguity lifecycle
description:
## Context
The full retry/ambiguity lifecycle — the part of keyval that makes "retry safety never expires" real end to end. This item accepts the attempt-table rows W14 deferred: conflict detection (incl. the in-flight same-ID different-command race), history-capacity refusal, live-quota terminal outcomes, attempt_state rules, and the read-only status endpoint.

## Requirements covered
F-6 (request IDs end to end), F-9 (status lookup: original terminal result if applied locally, else `unknown`; NEVER proposes; unknown never means "did not happen"), F-10 (every outcome distinguishable; terminal vs non-terminal), C-6, A-5, DM-7 (history admission).

## Area
`node/write_path`, `node/lifecycle`, `statemachine/history`.

## Depends on
W14 (controller), W27 (CAS/DELETE must exist for conflict-race coverage).

## Design & key rules
- Status endpoint (D-36): GET /v1/requests/{id} answered from the serving node's applied history in one turn; HTTP 200 with state known (embedded original terminal result — success, mismatch or capacity alike) or state unknown; never proposes; P8: a missing record is never evidence a write did not happen.
- In-flight same-ID different-command race (the §10.3 misuse case, deterministic in tests here): whichever command commits first is legitimately the original; the other resolves per apply step 3 as request_id_conflict; exactly ONE original and ONE conflict once both commands reach committed resolution, whichever command commits first. Timeouts and bounded-wait exhaustion still obey §7.8: they may remain unknown or busy, never report an unsupported terminal decision. Attach rules: same ID + same digest attaches (bounded, 16 waiters; shares the proposal's fate); same ID + different digest NEVER attaches — waits for the pending proposal to resolve, then is evaluated against committed history; if the pending proposal fails without applying, the waiter re-enters the F-7 order and may propose; if its bound expires with its command never proposed ⇒ 429 busy (not_submitted).
- History admission (DM-7): the leader refuses NEW mutations before proposal with 507 history_full once commit index ≥ max_log_entries OR committed first-execution command bytes (read at the leader's applied index) ≥ max_history_bytes. Reads, status lookups and retries of already-executed requests keep working. Protocol entries are never refused; the in-flight window can overshoot slightly — both are soft ceilings. Distinct from the terminal 507 capacity_exceeded (D-54).
- attempt_state discipline (A-5): not_submitted only for attempts never submitted; submitted for anything handed to consensus (or attached to a same-digest proposal); a later refusal never says anything about earlier attempts.

## Acceptance
- Status known/unknown; conflict detection end to end incl. the in-flight race (exactly one original, one conflict, whichever commits first); history-capacity refusal before proposal; live-quota terminal outcome; attempt_state rules; no status ever implies absence.

## Out of scope
HTTP handler wiring (W32); the capacity-profile sim heals (W43).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §7.8 (attach rows), F-9, DM-7, A-5, D-36, D-53, D-54, RISK-15.

title: W31: Independent black-box conformance suite
description:
## Context
The independent black-box API conformance suite: built OUTSIDE the server workspace, depending on no production crate, DTO or generated client (T-12); reads api/openapi.yaml and takes five base URLs. It may use the reference model and the K-10 witness from the oracle crates. This is the suite that will judge the real server in W32 — its own correctness is established FIRST against the model server and wrong-response fixtures.

## Requirements covered
T-12, §10.8.

## Area
`conformance` (top-level package).

## Depends on
W03 (spec), W30 (model server), W38 (K-10 witness for concurrent histories).

## Design & key rules
- Two test classes, tagged per test with class and targets (registry rows record them; nothing silently skipped): SEMANTIC tests (single-node behaviour) run against the model server, a real single node and every node of the real cluster; TOPOLOGY/LIFECYCLE tests (follower 307, no-leader 503, health during recovery) run only against the real cluster and may drive ./dev cluster kill|restart to create preconditions.
- Per-OPERATION target activation (D-70): a test runs against the model server once W30 closes, and against a real target only once the server wiring for every operation it exercises has landed (PUT/GET at W18; everything else and the cluster target at W32) — scheduled gates never demand functionality that does not exist yet.
- Stale-read discipline (C-7): a write-then-read semantic test POLLS the target node (bounded, timeout = failure) until served_by.applied_index ≥ the write's index before asserting values; staleness-tolerant assertions say so explicitly.
- Semantic, not just schema: each status must match its decision.
- Coverage list (§10.8): every operation on every node; redirects; no-leader 503 + node list; absent/deleted/re-created keys; same-value writes; CAS absent/version + contention; identical and conflicting request IDs; delayed retries; status lookups known/unknown; boundary inputs (255/256/257-byte keys, multibyte, empty values, 64 KiB values, JSON-escaping expansion, keys with / ? &); malformed JSON, unknown/duplicate fields, bad request IDs; SCAN ordering/edges/continuation/caps; health during recovery; read metadata; Cache-Control: no-store on reads, status and health; concurrent histories judged by K-10.
- K-10 rule: every write driven to a terminal result first (bounded same-ID retries + status lookups, incl. after topology restarts); a write still unresolved when the witness runs ⇒ `incomplete`, which FAILS (never a silently-passing inconclusive; D-75).

## Acceptance
- Semantic tests pass against the model server; the suite FAILS against a deliberately wrong response fixture (proves teeth); every test tagged with class and targets; the dependency check proves independence.

## Out of scope
Running against the real cluster (W32 closes that loop); the witness implementation itself (W38).

title: W33: CLI — all operations, durable pending store, bounded retries
description:
## Context
The full `keyval` CLI: every API operation plus the durable PENDING STORE that makes client-side retry safety real. The CLI is also the living reference client: its behaviour (same-ID retries, redirect following, status resolution) is what the workload generator mimics (§10.3).

## Requirements covered
O-4 (CLI with atomic durable pending store), O-6 (--json), C-6.

## Area
`cli`.

## Depends on
W23 (CLI crate), W32 (complete server surface).

## Design & key rules
- Commands: put | get | delete | cas | scan | status <request-id> | pending | resume <request-id> | cluster | doctor, all with --json (versioned schemas).
- Pending store (D-59 — the order matters): for every write, BEFORE sending: write a temp file with the request ID and exact command, fsync the TEMP FILE, rename into place, fsync the CONTAINING DIRECTORY (the directory sync must FOLLOW the rename or the final name is not durable). Delete the record only after a terminal result. A crash or power loss between persist and response must never lose a pending record; `pending` and `resume` also recover leftover temp files from an interrupted persist.
- Retries: never generates a new ID for a retry; follows 307 redirects; backs off on busy/unavailable/recovering; retries unknown_outcome with the SAME ID; bounds: 10 attempts, 5 distinct nodes, 15 s overall — exhaustion prints the request as UNRESOLVED with resume instructions; an unresolved request is NEVER reported as failed (RISK-15).

## Acceptance
- Every operation and status command works; the pending store persists atomically and durably before sending, with crash tests (kill between persist and send, and between response and delete) losing no record; resume never creates a new ID; redirects and retries stay within bounds; --json schemas validate.

## Out of scope
Doctor (done, W23); workload generator (W36 mimics this behaviour).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §8.7, O-4, D-59, RISK-15.
acceptance_criteria: Every operation works; pending store persists atomically+durably before sending with crash tests losing no record; resume never creates a new ID; redirects/retries within bounds; --json validates

title: W36: Workload generator and observation recording
description:
## Context
The workload generator: seeded simulated clients that behave like the real CLI, recorded as observations in W10's schema. Realistic contention and retry behaviour is what gives the checkers something meaningful to judge — a workload that never contends or retries proves nothing.

## Requirements covered
§10.3.

## Area
`sim/workload` (leaf area).

## Depends on
W10 (observation schema), W17 (composition root to drive).

## Design & key rules (condensed from §10.3)
- Clients: 1–8 per run (from the seed). Keys: 4–32 primary keys; ≥ half of writes target a small hot subset (contention); keys include ordering edge cases (a, aa, b), non-ASCII UTF-8, composed AND decomposed forms of the same text, / ? & % characters, maximum byte length. Values: empty strings, repeated same-value writes, maximum size, JSON-expansion-heavy values.
- Mix: ~30% PUT, 15% DELETE, 25% CAS, 20% GET, 10% SCAN; the mix varies by scenario (this item ships the PUT/GET profiles; full-op profiles are W43).
- Client behaviour (same as the CLI): one request ID + one exact command per logical write, kept for all retries; follow not_leader redirects; back off on busy/unavailable/recovering; retry unknown_outcome and lost responses with the SAME ID; sometimes resolve via the status endpoint instead; CAS typically uses the version from a recent GET (real read-modify-write races).
- Misuse stream: reuses a request ID with a DIFFERENT command, sent only after the original has a client-observed terminal result (the in-flight race is W29's deterministic territory, not this random stream); expected request_id_conflict; never counted as a logical write.
- History: every attempt's invocation time, completion time, target node, request and outcome recorded as observations (K-10's food).

## Acceptance
- Histories recorded in W10's observation schema; same-ID retries after lost responses; edge-case keys and values; PUT/GET profiles run.

## Out of scope
Fault injection (W37); DELETE/CAS/SCAN/capacity profiles (W43).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.3.
acceptance_criteria: Histories recorded in the observation schema; same-ID retries after lost responses; edge-case keys and values; PUT/GET profiles run

title: W37: Nemesis, swarm configurations, scenario files, heal protocol
description:
## Context
The nemesis (fault injector), swarm testing and the heal protocol — the machinery that turns the simulator into an evidence factory. Swarm testing (each seed choosing WHICH fault types are enabled and at what intensity) finds bugs uniform random faults miss.

## Requirements covered
§9.1 (every in-scope fault), §10.4 (nemesis/swarm/coverage), T-10 (scenario files), A-4 (heal/convergence).

## Area
`sim/nemesis` (leaf area).

## Depends on
W12 (disk faults), W16 (network faults), W17 (root), W36 (workload to run during chaos).

## Design & key rules
- Fault vocabulary (§9.1): crash-restart (volatile loss; seed-chosen prefix survival incl. garbage tails; random restart delay; stale completions sometimes delivered to the new incarnation); all-node crash (disks intact, possibly repeated); permanent loss (≤ 2 nodes; all ten pairs required); symmetric partitions (3/2, 4/1, 2/2/1, old leader on minority side); asymmetric partitions (leader sends-not-receives, reverse, directed cycles); message loss (incl. client-response paths — losing the reply after a committed application); delay/reorder; duplication; pause/stall (GC-style: keeps memory, inputs queue; pausing the leader past an election timeout then resuming into a newer term).
- Run phases (§10.2): Setup (scenario from seed) → Baseline (elect + a few successful writes BEFORE any fault) → Chaos (workload + nemesis, default 1,200 ticks) → Heal (stop faults; restart every recoverable node; restore links; clients resolve every outstanding logical write with their own IDs; then ONE uniquely-identified catch-up-marker PUT; wait until every recoverable node applied it; budget 600 ticks) → Check. The heal NEVER edits logs, forces elections, teleports state or drops outstanding requests. (Capacity-profile heal adaptations are W43's.)
- Swarm: each seed picks a non-empty fault-type subset + intensity (low/med/high); a no-fault control profile exists; the chosen subset and parameters go into the manifest.
- Liveness guard: the nemesis never leaves the cluster permanently without a quorum during Heal.
- Scenario files (T-10): a seed deterministically generates a scenario (swarm config, fault schedule, client plans); scenario + seed fully determines a run; serialises human-readable; a scenario file reproduces its seed's run exactly.
- Healthy envelope (§9.4) enforced BY CONSTRUCTION by the generator: ≥ 3 voters up/connected post-heal, 50 ms link bound, 20 ms sync bound, fair turns, ≤ 64 unresolved writes, bounded recovery/replication backlog, no surviving node at its journal hard stop. A run reporting `scenario invalid` maps to incomplete and FAILS (generator defect, D-73).

## Acceptance
- Every in-scope fault triggered, incl. partial unsynced survival, a lost sync completion, a stale completion after restart, pauses, all ten permanent-loss pairs and an all-node crash; a scenario file reproduces its seed's run exactly; heal resolves outstanding writes and commits the catch-up marker (capacity-profile adaptations accepted in W43).

## Out of scope
Coverage-matrix accounting (W41); capacity heals and full-op profiles (W43); shrinking (W44).

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §9.1, §9.4, §10.2 (phases), §10.4, T-10.

title: W38: Write-history checkers K-1, K-2, K-3, K-4 and the K-10 witness
description:
## Context
The write-history checkers: the oracles that judge durability, exactly-once, real-time order, result correctness and linearizability from recorded observations — in a separate crate depending on NO production crate (T-12), never computing expected results by calling production code.

## Requirements covered
C-1, C-2, C-5, C-6, DM-3; checkers K-1, K-2, K-3, K-4, K-10 (§10.5).

## Area
`checker/write_hist` (leaf area).

## Depends on
W10 (model + observation schema), W36 (recorded histories).

## Design & key rules
- K-1 Durability: every write acknowledged as SUCCESS has its first execution in the final committed log, at its reported index, with the reported effect, on every recoverable node — after crashes, all-node restarts, loss of ≤ 2 nodes. A later legitimate overwrite is fine (the check is on committed history, not final value).
- K-2 Exactly-once: each request ID has ≤ 1 first execution; every terminal EXECUTION response for that ID (excluding request_id_conflict answers to misuse and non-terminal refusals) reports the same index and decision; a conflicting reuse has no effect on any key. Independent of caches and attempt counts.
- K-3 Real-time order: over LOGICAL writes (attempts collapsed by request ID): if A's first terminal decision was observed before B's first invocation, then index(A) < index(B). A later retry legitimately returns its original smaller index — never a violation.
- K-4 Write results: replaying the committed log through the REFERENCE MODEL reproduces every reported write result (versions, existed, CAS results with correct current version, capacity outcomes, conflicts).
- K-10 Linearizability witness (BLACK-BOX; also used by conformance and v2 real-process testing): using only client observations — collapse attempts per request ID; take reported indices as an UNTRUSTED candidate order (reject collisions); run the model in that order comparing every result; place each write within its real-time interval by a greedy earliest-placement pass. The interval runs from first invocation to the first client-observed TERMINAL decision (unknown doesn't close it; a later replay is an observation, not a new write). Consumes the RESOLVED history. POLYNOMIAL time — no exponential search; must handle a 10,000-operation history.

## Acceptance
- Hand-made passing AND failing history fixtures for each checker (incl. legal overwrites and a lost acknowledged write); K-10 runs in polynomial time on a 10,000-operation history; each registered with marker + selector + min_cases.

## Out of scope
Read/convergence/liveness checkers (W39), Raft-level checkers (W40), non-vacuity (W41).

## Notes for the future
These checkers are the designated catchers for bug variants B-01 (ack at proposal), B-08/B-09 (CAS misevaluation), B-10/B-11/B-12/B-13 (dedup bugs), B-14 (version reset) — W45 will verify each catch. The negative-history corpus (fixed failing fixtures) is protected (P9): gate receipts hash it.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.5 (K-1..K-4, K-10), T-12, D-13, D-21.

title: W39: Read, convergence and liveness checkers K-5, K-6, K-7, K-9
description:
## Context
The read-side, convergence and liveness checkers: stale-but-committed reads, per-incarnation monotonicity, post-heal convergence, and progress within the healthy envelope.

## Requirements covered
C-3, C-4, C-8, A-1, A-2, A-3, A-4; checkers K-5, K-6, K-7, K-9 (§10.5).

## Area
`checker/reads` (leaf area).

## Depends on
W10 (model), W36 (observations), W37 (heal protocol produces what K-7/K-9 judge).

## Design & key rules
- K-5 Read validity: every GET, SCAN page and status lookup equals the MODEL's state at the committed prefix [1..applied_index] reported in served_by, and that prefix had actually been applied AND COMMITTED at the serving node before it answered (god view) — a read cannot borrow a prefix created after its response. For SCAN: order, uniqueness, range edges, item/byte caps, has_more/next_after all judged against that one prefix (K-5 implements the page-cap formula INDEPENDENTLY — T-12).
- K-6 Read monotonicity: per node INCARNATION, reported applied_index never decreases in controller response-GENERATION order (from the trace), not client-arrival order — network reordering of in-flight responses is not a violation.
- K-7 Convergence: after Heal, every recoverable node applied the catch-up marker with an IDENTICAL state digest (map + request history), computed AT EACH NODE'S APPLICATION OF THE MARKER (trailing election no-ops legitimately leave final applied indices unequal). DM-7 capacity profiles judge by identical commit/applied/digest over the quiet period instead (W43). Permanently lost nodes excluded and LISTED. Physical journals need not be byte-identical.
- K-9 Liveness: within the healthy envelope — every outstanding logical write reaches a terminal result and the marker commits within the heal budget (600 ticks). Capacity profiles follow the adapted completion rules.

## Acceptance
- Fixtures incl. a read borrowing a future prefix, a SCAN across two prefixes, a read-availability fixture (ready minority nodes serve; non-ready answer recovering), and permanent-loss exclusions; each registered.

## Notes for the future
Designated catchers: K-5 for B-05/B-06/B-07; K-9/K-7 for B-18. The healthy envelope is a test-profile property, not a production promise — outside it the system must stay SAFE but no progress is promised.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.5 (K-5..K-7, K-9), §9.4, C-3/C-4/C-8, A-1..A-4.

title: W40: Raft, persistence and honesty checkers K-8, K-11, K-12
description:
## Context
The Raft-safety, persistence-ordering and honesty checkers — the white-box oracles over the god view and trace. K-8's commit-certificate rule is the subtlest oracle in the project: it encodes WHY an old-term entry on three disks is not committed (the §5.4.2 trap from the Raft paper).

## Requirements covered
C-1, C-2, DUR-2, A-5; checkers K-8, K-11, K-12 (§10.5).

## Area
`checker/raft` (leaf area).

## Depends on
W10, W13 (semantics being checked), W14, W15 (trace/god view), W36.

## Design & key rules
- K-8 Raft safety (on the god view after EVERY step): election safety (≤ 1 leader per term; overlapping beliefs in different terms allowed); log matching (on entry bytes and term, not value hashes); leader completeness; state-machine safety; leader append-only. Commitment judged by COMMIT CERTIFICATES: an entry of term T durably accepted from the term-T leader by a majority DURING TERM T (the god view records the acceptance term per replica), plus the prefix before it. An old-term entry on three disks is NOT thereby committed. Certificates survive the later loss of a certifying node.
- K-11 Persistence ordering: from the trace — every vote grant, append acknowledgement, client success and published read depends only on durability obligations already satisfied (sync completed for the relevant term, vote and entries). Catches early releases DETERMINISTICALLY, without needing an unlucky crash. Obligations are DUR-2's: entries, term, vote — NEVER the commit index.
- K-12 Unknown-outcome honesty: no response after submission reports a guessed success or failure; not_submitted appears only for never-submitted attempts; status unknown never coincides with a claim of absence; every unresolved logical write is eventually resolved or reported unresolved.

## Acceptance
- Commit-certificate fixtures (an old-term entry on three disks is NOT committed); a vote-before-sync trace is detected; a guessed failure is detected; K-12 consumes W10's observation schema and W36's client observations; each registered.

## Notes for the future
Designated catchers: K-8 for B-16 (double vote across restart); K-11 for B-02/B-03/B-17; K-12 for B-15; K-11/K-1 jointly for early-release classes. K-8 judges on bytes+terms so it cannot be fooled by value-equal entries.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.5 (K-8, K-11, K-12), §3.2 (commit rule), D-44.

title: W41: Non-vacuity (K-13), coverage matrix, run verdicts
description:
## Context
Non-vacuity and coverage: the machinery that makes "it passed" mean something. An all-timeout run is a failure, not evidence of safety (P10). Coverage is measured by matrix cells, never by seed counts (§9.3: "seed counts are not coverage").

## Requirements covered
T-13, P10; checker K-13 (§10.16); the coverage matrix (§10.4); run verdicts (§10.2 outputs).

## Area
`checker/vacuity`, `sim`, `registry` (coverage.toml structure).

## Depends on
W37 (nemesis/phases), W38, W39, W40 (all checkers must exist to enforce "every applicable checker executed").

## Design & key rules
- K-13 marks a run `incomplete` (which FAILS) unless ALL of: successful writes before the first fault; ≥ 1 injected instance of EVERY selected fault type (a `scenario invalid` report itself fails as incomplete — generator defect); reads served by > 1 node (five-node profiles; scripted 1/3-voter profiles require reads from every voter); a successful post-heal write (the marker; DM-6/DM-7 adaptations per W43); a terminal resolution for every admitted logical write or a liveness failure; every applicable checker executed; event budget not exhausted.
- Overall verdict per run: pass | fail | incomplete (incomplete fails).
- Coverage matrix (per build): counts for each fault type, fault-type pair, partition topology (3/2, 4/1, 2/2/1, asymmetric cycle), crash point (§9.1), outcome (success, mismatch, conflict, live-capacity, history-full, unknown, not_leader, busy, unavailable, recovering) and operation. T2 reports empty cells; T3 requires every cell of the REQUIRED SET (enumerated in registry/coverage.toml — structure authored here, operation/outcome cells completed by W43) non-zero.
- Coverage JSON + `./dev report coverage` renderer.

## Acceptance
- An all-timeout run fails; an unexercised selected fault gives incomplete; budget exhaustion fails; coverage JSON produced and the report renders; registry/coverage.toml required-set structure authored.

PLAN.md wins over this bead (§0.4). Plan refs: §10.16, §10.4, P10, D-73.

title: W42: sim commands, crash packs, corpus runner
description:
## Context
The sim tooling agents live by: full `./dev sim` commands, crash packs for every failure, and the regression-corpus runner. A failing seed an agent cannot replay is worthless; a crash pack makes every failure a self-contained diagnosis kit (D-23).

## Requirements covered
T-4 (every failure replayable with one command), T-8 (crash packs), O-6.

## Area
`sim`.

## Depends on
W41 (verdicts determine what a "failure" is).
